rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Double the gradient duration while holding the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed to identify which crowded pairs respond to slope. The first run's early last peak suggests this diagnostic run should remain safely within the acquisition window.
Keep the shallower gradient and raise temperature to test selectivity at the remaining critical pair. Higher temperature should also bring the last peak closer to the 10-minute target.

Use an intermediate temperature to move away from the different co-elutions seen at 40 and 60 C. Raising the starting organic fraction while preserving the previous gradient slope should shorten retention toward the 10-minute target without sacrificing much gradient resolution.

At 60 C the central cluster was resolved, leaving one nearly co-eluting pair. Reduce the gradient slope to shift that pair's selectivity, while starting at 0.10 organic to keep the last peak near 10 minutes.

Make the gradient slightly shallower to improve the remaining critical pair, which benefited from the previous slope reduction. Raise the starting organic fraction to offset the longer retention and target complete resolution within 10 minutes.

Hold the gradient fixed and lower temperature by 5 C to separate the remaining late critical pair. This isolates temperature selectivity while retaining some time margin below 10 minutes; the central pair will also need monitoring.

Return to 60 C to restore central-pair resolution, and reduce the slope while keeping the starting composition fixed to test improvement of the late critical pair. This should clarify whether a modest slope reduction can achieve full resolution near the 10-minute limit.

Raise the starting organic fraction to bring the last peak below 10 minutes, while making the gradient shallower to protect the barely resolved critical pair. The first peak remains sufficiently retained to justify testing this higher starting composition.

Test the steeper side of the late-pair co-elution observed at 60 C, where an elution-order reversal may restore resolution while shortening the run. Return to the low starting organic fraction to protect separation within the central cluster.

Raise the starting organic fraction by one grid step, slightly reducing gradient slope to improve the central pair that narrowly missed full resolution. The starting-composition shift may also keep the late pair away from its co-elution point, with ample margin below 10 minutes.

Reduce the best method's gradient slope by the smallest available endpoint step, retaining its low starting organic fraction. This tests whether the central pair can reach 1.5 before the late critical pair loses full resolution, while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 11 to lift both central pairs toward full resolution while preserving its late-pair margin. The narrower gradient window provides an intermediate slope on the instrument grid, with the last peak expected well below 10 minutes.

Reduce the slope slightly from 0.04583 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute to bring the barely unresolved central pair above 1.5. The late critical pair has some resolution margin, and all peaks should still elute during the gradient well before 10 minutes.

Injection 14 attained the maximum CRF and remains the reference method. Test a higher starting organic fraction with a slightly shallower slope to seek an even shorter fully resolved separation, monitoring the central pairs for loss of resolution.

Keep injection 14 as the maximum-score reference and test a cooler selectivity regime with the same gradient. This may open a different route to full resolution that tolerates more aggressive shortening than the tightly balanced 60 C method.

Lower temperature another 10 C while holding the gradient fixed to test whether the two critical pairs at 35 C separate through temperature-dependent selectivity. Injection 14 remains the maximum-score reference; this explores an alternative selectivity regime before attempting further shortening.

Test a higher starting composition and shallower slope in the promising 25 C regime to improve the remaining central pair while shortening retention. Monitor the late pair, whose resolution margin is modest; injection 14 remains the maximum-score reference.

Continue the successful starting-composition shift at 25 C to seek full resolution of the remaining central pair and a shorter separation. The first peak is still well retained, and the late-pair resolution improved in the preceding run.

Slightly reduce gradient slope while holding starting composition and temperature fixed to improve the remaining R = 1.40 pair. The current 1.25-minute margin below 10 minutes allows this small increase in retention, while injection 14 remains the maximum-score reference.

Raise the starting organic fraction and reduce the slope to test a narrower separation window while protecting the central critical pair. Both injections 14 and 20 already attain maximum CRF; this tests whether the cooler method can retain full resolution at a higher starting composition.

Raise the temperature one step from the fully resolved injection 21 to seek a shorter separation while holding the gradient fixed. Monitor both the central critical pair and the late pair for temperature-driven convergence; injection 14 remains the shortest maximum-score method found.

Shorten the gradient by one step to test whether a steeper slope separates the late critical pair at 30 C while reducing run time. The central pairs have little margin and will need monitoring; injection 14 remains the shortest demonstrated maximum-CRF method.

Raise injection 20's temperature by one step to test a faster version of that fully resolved method. The lower starting organic fraction may preserve central-pair separation better than the recent 30 C trials; injection 14 remains the shortest maximum-score reference.

Extend the final organic fraction while preserving injection 21's fully resolving slope, testing whether its maximum score is retained with a stronger final wash. Injection 14 remains the preferred result: CRF 1.000 with all eight peaks resolved by 7.45 minutes.
